519.title: My peace I give (John 14:27)
519.hook: not as the world gives; said at every Mass before the sign of peace
519.howItsDone: At Mass, after the Our Father, the priest prays a prayer recalling John 14:27 and says, "The peace of the Lord be with you always"; then people may exchange a sign of peace with those near them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many mansions, and a place prepared for frightened friends. Your line was a place for you. Who did you make room for? Day five hundred nineteen.

Partway through Mass, a little after the Our Father, comes a moment when strangers turn to each other. A handshake across the pew. A nod to the teenager behind, a hug for a mother, a wave to someone too far away to reach. Peace be with you. Just before that moment, the priest says a short prayer that recalls a single sentence Jesus spoke at the Last Supper. It goes by quickly. Today we find it where it started.
screen: `STRANGERS TURN TO EACH OTHER.` → `PEACE BE WITH YOU.` → `A SENTENCE FROM THE SUPPER.`

segments.voice: Jesus is still at the table, telling his friends he's leaving. He's promised them the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who will teach them and remind them of everything. And then, like someone at a doorway saying goodbye, he leaves them a gift. In the Douay-Rheims: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, do I give unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid." Peace, shalom, was an everyday word of greeting; after Easter Jesus will greet these same friends with it: peace be to you. Here he takes that everyday word and fills it. My peace. Not as the world gives. How does the world give peace? Usually as an absence: no war, no noise, no problems, everything finally sorted out. Peace when the to-do list is done. Jesus says this to men who are about to watch him arrested, who will scatter in fear, who will hide behind locked doors. Nothing around them will be calm. Whatever his peace is, it isn't the absence of trouble. It's something given in the middle of it. Perhaps that's why the Church puts it where it does. Before the sign of peace, the priest addresses Christ, recalling that he said to the apostles, peace I leave you, my peace I give you, and asks him to look not on our sins but on the faith of his Church. Then the peace is passed, hand to hand. Not a feeling people work up, but a gift handed on.
screen: `A GOODBYE GIFT AT THE DOOR.` · `SHALOM, FILLED.` · `PEACE IN THE MIDDLE OF TROUBLE.` · `THE PRAYER BEFORE THE SIGN OF PEACE.` · then, large: `MY PEACE I GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive peace, then picture handing it on. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Notice whatever is unsettled today, and don't try to fix it. Breathe in as if you were being handed something, and out as if you were setting it down. Then think of one person you're tense with, or just haven't spoken to in a while. Picture turning to them, as at Mass, and offering your hand. If you pray, you can hold the line, my peace I give unto you. If you don't, just hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
My peace I give. Jesus's farewell gift at the supper: a peace not as the world gives, recalled at every Mass before the sign of peace. Today's word.
Your line: not as the world gives. Today, offer peace to that one person: a message, a handshake, a kind word, before things are sorted out. Day five hundred nineteen.

520.title: The vine (John 15:1–8)
520.hook: abide in me; without me you can do nothing
520.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray short aspirations through the day, a name or a single line such as "Jesus, Mary, Joseph," alongside longer prayer at Mass and at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell gift: my peace I give. Your line was not as the world gives. Did you offer peace to someone? Day five hundred twenty.

Cut a rose for a vase and it looks perfect for a day or two. Same color, same petals, same smell as the one still on the bush. But it's already on a clock. It has everything except a connection. Nothing is flowing into it anymore. At the end of chapter fourteen Jesus says, arise, let us go hence. Some readers picture them leaving the supper room and walking out into the dark. John doesn't say where they are. What he gives us next is a vine.
screen: `A CUT ROSE, ON A CLOCK.` → `ARISE, LET US GO HENCE.` → `A VINE.`

segments.voice: It's another of John's I am sayings, and the Douay-Rheims begins: "I am the true vine; and my Father is the husbandman." Husbandman is the old word for farmer, the one who tends the vines. In the Hebrew scriptures, Israel itself is pictured as God's vine, planted and cared for. Jesus takes the picture personally. Then the key verse: "I am the vine; you the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing." The word to hold is abide. In Greek it's menō, to stay, remain, live somewhere. It shows up again and again in these few verses. A branch doesn't produce fruit by straining. It doesn't try harder. It stays attached and the sap does the work. And there's a hard note too: the farmer prunes. Every branch that bears fruit, he cuts back, so it bears more. Anyone who's watched a grapevine pruned in winter knows how brutal it looks, bare stubs where there were long canes, and how much fruit comes that summer. Catholics hear the vine in two places especially. One is the Eucharist, the fruit of the vine on the altar. The other is the ordinary day. Some saints recommended very short prayers through the day, sometimes called aspirations: a name, a single line, said while washing dishes or waiting at a light, like Jesus, Mary, Joseph. Not a long prayer. Just staying connected.
screen: `ANOTHER I AM: THE TRUE VINE.` · `ABIDE: STAY, REMAIN, LIVE.` · `THE FARMER PRUNES.` · `SHORT PRAYERS THROUGH THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE VINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay. Sit, and notice the places where your body is connected to something: feet on the floor, back against the chair, hands resting. Let your weight be held. Breathe, and don't try to do anything. Just remain. If your mind wanders, come back to the contact points. If you pray, you can hold one short line from the Gospel, abide in me, and come back to it each time you drift. If you don't, simply stay where you are. The bell holds the time.
The vine. Jesus is the vine and his followers the branches: whoever abides in him bears much fruit. Today's word.
Your line: abide. Today, pick three ordinary moments, a red light, a sink, a door, and use each one to reconnect for a single breath. Day five hundred twenty.

521.title: Greater love (John 15:13)
521.hook: greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends
521.howItsDone: The Church keeps a yearly memorial of Saint Maximilian Kolbe, and John 15:13 is often read at the funerals of people who died serving others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vine and the branches. Your line was one word: abide. Which ordinary moments did you use to reconnect? Day five hundred twenty-one.

Greater love than this no man hath. The sentence has been carved in stone on war memorials, set on plaques for firefighters, read aloud in eulogies for nurses and soldiers. People reach for it when someone has given everything for someone else. Usually it stands alone, with no chapter around it. It sounds like it was written for a monument. It was actually said at a supper table, the night before the one who said it died.
screen: `A SENTENCE CARVED IN STONE.` → `FIREFIGHTERS, NURSES, SOLDIERS.` → `FIRST SAID AT A SUPPER TABLE.`

segments.voice: Jesus has just repeated his commandment: love one another as I have loved you. Then he explains what as I have loved you is going to mean. In the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." The Greek for life here is psychē, the word that also means soul, the whole self. And lay down is the same verb Jesus used about the good shepherd: I lay down my life for my sheep. It also echoes the supper itself. In chapter thirteen he laid down his garments to wash their feet, and took them up again. Lay down, take up. The towel and the cross are drawn in the same strokes. He's not describing a hero somewhere else. He's describing tomorrow afternoon. Catholics have a modern face for this verse. At Auschwitz, after a prisoner escaped, the guards chose men to starve to death in a bunker. One of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and children. A Franciscan priest, Maximilian Kolbe, stepped forward and asked to take his place. He was allowed to, and he died in that bunker. Gajowniczek survived the war and lived to see Pope John Paul the Second declare Kolbe a saint. But the verse isn't only about dying. A parent's sleep given up for years, a caregiver's evenings, a career paused for a sick friend: some readers see those too as a life laid down a little at a time.
screen: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU, MEANS THIS.` · `LAY DOWN: THE TOWEL, THE CROSS.` · `KOLBE STEPS FORWARD.` · `A LIFE LAID DOWN A LITTLE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `GREATER LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose something to give up for a friend. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring one friend to mind, someone who could use a hand right now. Then look at your own day and find something of yours to set down for them: an hour, a plan, a preference, the right to be right. Let it be real but small enough to actually do. Picture handing it over. If you pray, you can hold the line, greater love than this no man hath. If you don't, just hold your friend's face. The bell holds the time.
Greater love. Jesus at the supper: no one has greater love than to lay down their life for their friends. Today's word.
Your line: lay down your life. Today, give that one small thing away for your friend, and let it cost something. Day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: I have called you friends (John 15:15)
522.howItsDone: Many Catholics practice mental prayer, an unscripted conversation with God, often in silence before the tabernacle, alongside the set prayers of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greater love, and a life laid down for friends. Your line was lay down your life. What did you give up for someone? Day five hundred twenty-two.

There's a difference between an employee and a friend, and you can hear it in what you're told. An employee gets instructions: do this by Friday, here's the form. Whether they understand why is optional. A friend gets the story. Here's what's going on, here's what I'm worried about, here's why it matters. The tasks might even be the same. What's different is whether you're let in. Yesterday Jesus said the greatest love lays down its life for its friends. Then he tells the people at the table who those friends are.
screen: `AN EMPLOYEE GETS INSTRUCTIONS.` → `A FRIEND GETS THE STORY.` → `WHO ARE THE FRIENDS?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "I will not now call you servants: for the servant knoweth not what his lord doth. But I have called you friends: because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you." Notice the reason he gives. Not, because you've earned it. Not, because you're equals. Because I've told you everything. Friendship, here, is defined by being let in on what the Father is doing. Servant in the Greek is doulos, often meaning a slave, someone who simply carries out orders. Being called God's servant was already an honor in the scriptures: Moses was called the servant of the Lord. And yet there's an older word too. Abraham was called the friend of God, in Isaiah and again in the letter of James. Jesus offers that same title to a table of fishermen and a tax collector. He doesn't drop the commands, mind you. The verse just before says, you are my friends if you do the things I command you. Friends still do what's asked. They just know why. This picture of friendship runs deep in the way many Catholics pray. Saint Teresa of Ávila, the sixteenth-century Carmelite, described mental prayer as close, friendly conversation, often alone, with the one we know loves us. Not a speech to a distant king. A conversation with a friend who has already told you his secrets. That's the move today: from following orders to being let in.
screen: `NOT SERVANTS: FRIENDS.` · `BECAUSE I'VE TOLD YOU EVERYTHING.` · `ABRAHAM, THE FRIEND OF GOD.` · `TERESA: PRAYER AS FRIENDSHIP.` · then, large: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk the way you'd talk to a friend. Sit somewhere comfortable, the way you would across from someone you trust. Breathe. Then, instead of formal words, say plainly, inside, what today has actually been like: what went well, what's bothering you, what you're not sure about. No speeches. If you pray, you can say it to God, the way Teresa described, as to a friend who loves you. If you don't, simply tell it to the quiet, honestly. Then listen for a while. The bell holds the time.
I have called you friends. Jesus at the supper: not servants who only get orders, but friends who've been told everything. Today's word.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: friends, not servants. Today, tell someone you work with or live with the why behind something, not just the what. Day five hundred twenty-two.

523.title: The Spirit of truth (John 16:12–15)
523.hook: I have many things to say but you cannot bear them now
523.howItsDone: Catholics pray to the Holy Spirit for understanding, especially at Pentecost and before study or decisions, often with the traditional prayer "Come, Holy Spirit."

segments.voice: Yesterday, I have called you friends: the ones who are told everything. Your line was friends, not servants. Who did you tell the why to? Day five hundred twenty-three.

A good doctor doesn't read you the whole chart in the first five minutes. A good parent doesn't explain everything about death to a four-year-old at bedtime. A good teacher doesn't start calculus on the first day of algebra. Not because they're hiding something, but because there's an order to understanding. Some things you can only carry when you're ready. Yesterday Jesus said he'd told his friends everything he heard from the Father. Today, still at the table, he says something that sounds like the opposite.
screen: `NOT THE WHOLE CHART AT ONCE.` → `AN ORDER TO UNDERSTANDING.` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth." So which is it? Has he told them everything, or not? Both, in a way. Everything has been given in him. But they can't carry it all yet. Bear is a carrying word, the kind you'd use for a heavy load. It's honest about the disciples. These are men who, within hours, will fall asleep in the garden and run. They're not ready for the whole of it, and Jesus doesn't pretend they are. So he promises the Spirit of truth, who will teach them, or in the Greek, guide them, lead them along the way, into all the truth. Not dump it on them. Walk them into it. And the Spirit, Jesus says, won't bring a new message of his own. He'll take what is mine and show it to you. Catholics hear in this promise the Church's long, slow understanding of what it received. The Second Vatican Council taught that the understanding of what has been handed down grows over time, through contemplation, study and the experience of believers. In the nineteenth century John Henry Newman, now a canonized saint, wrote a whole book on how doctrine develops, the way a living thing grows up without turning into something else. Not new revelation, the Church says, but deeper understanding of what was given. Not yet, but coming.
screen: `YOU CANNOT BEAR THEM NOW.` · `HE WILL GUIDE YOU INTO ALL TRUTH.` · `NOT NEW: WHAT IS MINE, SHOWN.` · `NEWMAN: DOCTRINE GROWS LIKE A LIFE.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT OF TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a question wait. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you don't understand yet, about your faith, your life, a person, a loss. Don't try to solve it. Imagine setting it on a table in front of you, not thrown away, just set down to come back to later. Notice whether your shoulders loosen a little. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's promise, he will teach you all truth, and leave the question with him. If you don't, simply let it rest on the table. The bell holds the time.
The Spirit of truth. Jesus's promise that the Spirit will guide his friends into the truth they can't yet carry. Today's word.
Your line: not yet, but coming. Today, when you hit something you don't understand, say not yet, instead of never. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: Sorrow into joy (John 16:20–22)
524.hook: like a woman in labor, whose sorrow turns to joy
524.carry: your joy no man shall take
524.tomorrow: That they all may be one
524.howItsDone: Catholics keep Lent and the Easter Triduum, then the Easter season of rejoicing, which runs through to Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spirit of truth, who leads into what we can't yet carry. Your line was not yet, but coming. Where did you say not yet instead of never? Day five hundred twenty-four.

Ask anyone who has given birth, or stood in a delivery room beside someone who has. The hours before are hard to describe and harder to sit through. And then, almost in the same minute, the room changes. The baby is crying, someone is laughing, someone is texting a photo to the whole family. Hours of pain, and then something that doesn't erase the pain so much as outweigh it. Jesus is still at the supper, and his friends are confused. A little while, he keeps saying, and you won't see me. To explain, he reaches for a birth.
screen: `THE HOURS BEFORE.` → `THEN THE ROOM CHANGES.` → `A LITTLE WHILE.`

segments.voice: The disciples are whispering among themselves: what does he mean, a little while? Jesus hears them and answers straight. You will weep and lament, and the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "your sorrow shall be turned into joy." Notice it doesn't say replaced. It says turned. The same sorrow becomes the joy, the way the labor itself becomes the birth. Then the picture. A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow because her hour has come. That word again, hour, the word John uses for the cross. But when the child is born, she doesn't remember the anguish anymore, for joy that a person has come into the world. And he finishes: "So also you now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice; and your joy no man shall take from you." At Easter, they'll see him again. That's the first meaning. But the Church has read it more widely. Joy, in this picture, isn't the absence of grief. It's on the far side of it, and it's not fragile, no one can take it. Catholics live this in the rhythm of the year: the fast of Lent, the sorrow of Good Friday, and then an Easter season that runs all the way to Pentecost. And some who have walked through a real loss describe something like it: the grief didn't go away, but it was turned, slowly, into something they wouldn't give back.
screen: `A LITTLE WHILE, AND YOU WEEP.` · `NOT REPLACED: TURNED.` · `THE WOMAN IN LABOR.` · `JOY NO ONE CAN TAKE.` · then, large: `SORROW INTO JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on. Sit, and breathe slowly and steadily, the way a birth coach counts breaths. In for four, out for six. If you're in a painful season right now, let yourself name it, quietly. You don't have to make it mean anything yet. Just breathe through it, one breath at a time, the way people do through labor. If you're not in one, hold someone who is. If you pray, you can hold the line, your sorrow shall be turned into joy. If you don't, just keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Sorrow into joy. Jesus's promise at the supper: grief, like labor, turned into a joy no one can take. Today's word.
Your line: your joy no man shall take. Today, notice one small joy, a laugh, a taste, a voice, and keep it. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: That they all may be one (John 17:20–23)
525.word: That they all may be one
525.hook: his prayer for unity, the charter of Christian unity work
525.howItsDone: Each January, Catholics in many places join Orthodox and Protestant Christians in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and the Mass includes prayers for the unity of Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sorrow turned into joy, like labor into birth. Your line was your joy no man shall take. What small joy did you keep? Day five hundred twenty-five.

On a single street in many towns you can find a Catholic parish, a Baptist church, a Greek Orthodox church and a Lutheran one, each with its own sign out front. Every Sunday they read from the same Gospels. Christians have been divided for a long time, some of the splits many centuries old, some newer. So it's striking to remember that, in John's Gospel, the last thing Jesus does before he walks out to the garden is pray out loud. And part of what he prays for is the people on that street.
screen: `FOUR CHURCHES, ONE STREET.` → `SPLITS CENTURIES OLD.` → `THE LAST THING HE DOES: PRAY.`

segments.voice: John seventeen is sometimes called the high priestly prayer. Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays for himself, then for the disciples at the table. Then he looks further: not for them only, but for those who will believe in me through their word. That's everyone after them. And here's what he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice the measure, again. Not one the way a club is one, or a company. One as the Father and the Son are one. And notice the reason: that the world may believe. Unity isn't a private comfort. It's a sign, the same way the new commandment was a sign. Catholics call efforts toward Christian unity ecumenism, and they point to this prayer as its charter. In 1964 the Second Vatican Council issued a decree on ecumenism, saying that division openly contradicts the will of Christ. In 1995 Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on Christian unity, and gave it this prayer's Latin as its title: Ut unum sint, that they may be one. Each January, in many places, Catholics, Orthodox and Protestant Christians keep a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity together. That's week seventy-five: my peace I give, the vine, greater love, friends, the Spirit of truth, sorrow into joy, and now, that they may be one.
screen: `THE HIGH PRIESTLY PRAYER.` · `FOR THOSE WHO WILL BELIEVE.` · `ONE AS THE FATHER AND SON.` · `UT UNUM SINT, 1995.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the divided church. Sit, and breathe. Picture the churches near you, not just your own, all of them, the buildings and the people inside. Picture someone you love who worships somewhere different, or who stopped going. Don't argue anything in your head. Just hold them all together, side by side. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own words for them, that they all may be one. If you don't, simply hold the picture of them gathered in one place. The bell holds the time.
That they all may be one. Jesus's prayer the night before he died, for all who would believe, that their unity would be a sign to the world. Today's word.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE — today's word`.

fork.setup: it's your last evening with your friends. you pray out loud for the people who will believe because of them, centuries later. what do you ask for?

that they'll be safe from harm.
fork.reveal: that they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee, that the world may believe.

original.note: Greek: that they all may be one (John 17:21). Latin: ut omnes unum sint.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wish that Christians would get along.
what it means: a prayer for a unity modeled on the Father and Son, meant as a sign so the world may believe.
what a scholar hears: the Greek is hina pantes hen ōsin; its Latin, ut unum sint, gave John Paul II's 1995 encyclical its name.
